questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One mole of diatomic gas having rotational modes only is kept in a cylinder with a piston system. The cross-section area of the cylinder is $4$ cm$^2$. The gas is heated slowly to raise the temperature by $1.2\,^\circ$C during which the piston moves by $25$ mm. The amount of heat supplied to the gas is ________ J. (Atmospheric pressure $=100$ kPa, $R=8.3$ J/mol·K) (Neglect mass of the piston)
questions.solution:
Using the first law of thermodynamics:
$Q = \Delta U + W$

Since the gas is diatomic with rotational modes only, the degrees of freedom are $f = 5$, so:
$C_V = \dfrac{5}{2}R$

For $n = 1\text{ mole}$ and $\Delta T = 1.2\text{ K}$:
$\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T = 1 \times \dfrac{5}{2} \times 8.3 \times 1.2 = 24.9\text{ J}$

Work done by the gas:
$W = P\,\Delta V$

Cross-sectional area of the piston:
$A = 4\text{ cm}^2 = 4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$

Piston displacement:
$x = 25\text{ mm} = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$

Change in volume:
$\Delta V = A \cdot x = (4 \times 10^{-4})(2.5 \times 10^{-2}) = 1 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3$

With $P = 100\text{ kPa} = 10^5\text{ Pa}$:
$W = (10^5)(1 \times 10^{-5}) = 1\text{ J}$

Therefore, the heat supplied is:
$Q = \Delta U + W = 24.9 + 1 = 25.9\text{ J}$

Hence, the heat supplied to the gas is $25.9\text{ J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Initial pressure and volume of a monoatomic ideal gas are $P$ and $V$. The change in internal energy of this gas in adiabatic expansion to volume $V_{final}=27V$ is ________ J.
questions.solution:
For a monoatomic ideal gas, the ratio of specific heats is $\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}$.

In an adiabatic process, $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$.

$P_1 V_1^{\gamma} = P_2 V_2^{\gamma}$

$P V^{5/3} = P_2 (27V)^{5/3}$

$P_2 = P \left(\dfrac{1}{27}\right)^{5/3} = \dfrac{P}{243}$

The change in internal energy is given by:

$\Delta U = \dfrac{P_2 V_2 - P_1 V_1}{\gamma - 1}$

Substituting the values:

$\Delta U = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{P}{243}\right)(27V) - PV}{\dfrac{5}{3} - 1}$

$\Delta U = \dfrac{\dfrac{PV}{9} - PV}{\dfrac{2}{3}}$

$\Delta U = \dfrac{-\dfrac{8}{9}PV}{\dfrac{2}{3}} = -\dfrac{4}{3}PV$

Answer: $-\dfrac{4}{3}PV$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cylinder with adiabatic walls is closed at both ends and is divided into two compartments by a frictionless adiabatic piston. Ideal gas is filled in both (left and right) the compartments at same $P, V, T$. Heating is started from left side until pressure changes to $\dfrac{27P}{8}$. If initial volume of each compartment was $9$ litres then the final volume in right-hand side compartment is __________ litres. (for this ideal gas $C_P/C_V = 1.5$)
questions.solution:
The right compartment is enclosed by adiabatic walls and an adiabatic piston, and no heat is supplied to it. Therefore, the gas in the right compartment undergoes an adiabatic compression.

Since the piston is frictionless, the pressure in the right compartment is always equal to the pressure in the left compartment. The final pressure in both compartments is $P_f = \dfrac{27P}{8}$.

For the adiabatic process in the right compartment, the equation is:
$P_i V_i^\gamma = P_f V_f^\gamma$

Given $P_i = P$, $V_i = 9$ L, $P_f = \dfrac{27P}{8}$, and $\gamma = \dfrac{C_P}{C_V} = 1.5 = \dfrac{3}{2}$. Substituting these values:
$P(9)^{3/2} = \left(\dfrac{27P}{8}\right) V_f^{3/2}$

Since $9^{3/2} = (3^2)^{3/2} = 3^3 = 27$, the equation becomes:
$27P = \dfrac{27P}{8} V_f^{3/2}$

Dividing both sides by $27P$:
$1 = \dfrac{1}{8} V_f^{3/2}$

$V_f^{3/2} = 8$

Taking the power of $2/3$ on both sides:
$V_f = (8)^{2/3} = (2^3)^{2/3} = 2^2 = 4$ litres.

Answer: $4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two closed vessels of same volume are joined through a narrow tube and both vessels are filled with air of pressure $90$ kPa and temperature $400$ K. Keeping the temperature of one vessel constant at $400$ K the second vessel temperature is raised to $500$ K. The final pressure in the vessels is _______ kPa.
questions.solution:
Let the volume of each vessel be $V$.

Initially, both vessels are at pressure $P_1 = 90$ kPa and temperature $T_1 = 400$ K.

Total number of moles initially is given by:

$n_i = \dfrac{P_1 V}{R T_1} + \dfrac{P_1 V}{R T_1} = \dfrac{2 P_1 V}{R T_1}$

Finally, the temperature of the first vessel is $T_1 = 400$ K and the second vessel is $T_2 = 500$ K. Let the final pressure be $P_f$.

Total number of moles finally is given by:

$n_f = \dfrac{P_f V}{R T_1} + \dfrac{P_f V}{R T_2}$

Since the total number of moles remains constant, $n_i = n_f$:

$\dfrac{2 P_1 V}{R T_1} = \dfrac{P_f V}{R T_1} + \dfrac{P_f V}{R T_2}$

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{2 \times 90}{400} = \dfrac{P_f}{400} + \dfrac{P_f}{500}$

$\dfrac{180}{400} = P_f \left( \dfrac{1}{400} + \dfrac{1}{500} \right)$

$\dfrac{180}{400} = P_f \left( \dfrac{5 + 4}{2000} \right)$

$\dfrac{180}{400} = P_f \left( \dfrac{9}{2000} \right)$

$P_f = \dfrac{180 \times 2000}{400 \times 9}$

$P_f = 20 \times 5 = 100$ kPa

Answer: $100$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A certain gas is isothermally compressed to $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{rd}$ of its initial volume ($V_o = 3$ litre) by applying required pressure. If the bulk modulus of the gas is $3 \times 10^5$ N/m$^2$, the magnitude of work done on the gas is _______ J.
questions.solution:
For an isothermal process, the isothermal bulk modulus equals the gas pressure:
$B_T = -V\dfrac{dP}{dV}$

Since $PV = \text{constant}$, differentiating gives $P\,dV + V\,dP = 0$, so $\dfrac{dP}{dV} = -\dfrac{P}{V}$, which yields $B_T = P$.

Therefore, the initial pressure is:
$P_o = 3 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}^2$

Volumes:
$V_o = 3\text{ L} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$
$V_f = \dfrac{1}{3}V_o = 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$

Work done on the gas during an isothermal compression:
$W_{\text{on}} = -W_{\text{by}} = -P_o V_o \ln\left(\dfrac{V_f}{V_o}\right) = P_o V_o \ln\left(\dfrac{V_o}{V_f}\right)$

$W_{\text{on}} = (3 \times 10^5)(3 \times 10^{-3})\ln 3$

$W_{\text{on}} = 900 \ln 3\text{ J}$

Using $\ln 3 \approx 1.0986$:
$W_{\text{on}} \approx 900 \times 1.0986 \approx 988.74\text{ J}$

Rounded to the nearest integer:
$W_{\text{on}} \approx 989\text{ J}$

Hence, the work done on the gas is approximately $989\text{ J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas at pressure $P$ and temperature $T$ is expanding such that $PT^3 = $ constant. The coefficient of volume expansion of the gas is _______.
questions.solution:
Given the process equation for the ideal gas:

$PT^3 = \text{constant}$

From the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT$, which gives $P = \dfrac{nRT}{V}$.

Substituting $P$ into the process equation:

$\left(\dfrac{nRT}{V}\right) T^3 = \text{constant}$

$\dfrac{T^4}{V} = \text{constant}$

$V = k T^4$

Differentiating both sides with respect to temperature $T$:

$\dfrac{dV}{dT} = 4k T^3$

The coefficient of volume expansion $\gamma$ is defined as:

$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V} \dfrac{dV}{dT}$

Substituting the values of $V$ and $\dfrac{dV}{dT}$:

$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{k T^4} (4k T^3) = \dfrac{4}{T}$

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{T}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
A. Zeroth law of thermodynamics gives concept of temperature
B. First law of thermodynamics gives concept of internal energy
C. In isothermal expansion of ideal gas, $\Delta Q \neq \Delta W$
D. Product of intensive and extensive variables is extensive
E. The ratio of any extensive variable to mass will be an extensive variable
Choose the correct combination of statements from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Statement A is correct because the zeroth law of thermodynamics defines temperature and thermal equilibrium.

Statement B is correct because the first law of thermodynamics introduces the concept of internal energy through the equation $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$.

Statement C is incorrect because for an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the change in internal energy $\Delta U = 0$. According to the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta Q = \Delta W$.

Statement D is correct because if an intensive variable (which is independent of the size of the system) is multiplied by an extensive variable (which is directly proportional to the size of the system), the product will be directly proportional to the size of the system, making it an extensive variable.

Statement E is incorrect because the ratio of two extensive variables (like any extensive variable and mass) is independent of the size of the system, making it an intensive variable.

Therefore, only statements A, B, and D are correct.

Answer: A, B and D Only

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas undergoes a process maintaining relation between pressure $(P)$ and volume $(V)$ as $P = P_o\left(1 + \left(\dfrac{V_o}{V}\right)^2\right)^{-1}$, where $P_o$ and $V_o$ are constants. If two samples $A$ and $B$ (two moles each) with initial volumes $V_o$ and $3V_o$ respectively undergo above mentioned process and attain same pressure, then the difference at the temperatures of these samples, $T_B - T_A$ is _____. ($R = $ gas constant)
questions.solution:
The given relation between pressure and volume is:

$P = P_o\left(1 + \left(\dfrac{V_o}{V}\right)^2\right)^{-1}$

For sample A, the initial volume is $V_A = V_o$. Substituting this into the given relation, the initial pressure $P_A$ is:

$P_A = P_o\left(1 + \left(\dfrac{V_o}{V_o}\right)^2\right)^{-1} = \dfrac{P_o}{2}$

Using the ideal gas equation $PV = nRT$ for $n = 2$ moles, the initial temperature $T_A$ is:

$T_A = \dfrac{P_A V_A}{nR} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{P_o}{2}\right) V_o}{2R} = \dfrac{P_o V_o}{4R}$

For sample B, the initial volume is $V_B = 3V_o$. Substituting this into the relation, the initial pressure $P_B$ is:

$P_B = P_o\left(1 + \left(\dfrac{V_o}{3V_o}\right)^2\right)^{-1} = P_o\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{9}\right)^{-1} = \dfrac{9P_o}{10}$

The initial temperature $T_B$ for $n = 2$ moles is:

$T_B = \dfrac{P_B V_B}{nR} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{9P_o}{10}\right) (3V_o)}{2R} = \dfrac{27P_o V_o}{20R}$

The difference in the initial temperatures of the two samples is:

$T_B - T_A = \dfrac{27P_o V_o}{20R} - \dfrac{P_o V_o}{4R}$

$T_B - T_A = \dfrac{27P_o V_o - 5P_o V_o}{20R} = \dfrac{22P_o V_o}{20R} = \dfrac{11P_o V_o}{10R}$

Answer: $\dfrac{11P_o V_o}{10R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $5$ moles of unknown gas is heated at constant volume from $10 \, °C$ to $20 \, °C$. The molar specific heat of this gas at constant pressure $c_p = 8$ cal/mol.°C and $R = 8.36$ J/mol.°C. The change in the internal energy of the gas is _______ calorie.
questions.solution:
Given $n = 5$ moles, $\Delta T = 20^{\circ}\text{C} - 10^{\circ}\text{C} = 10^{\circ}\text{C}$.

The molar specific heat at constant pressure is $c_p = 8 \text{ cal/mol}\cdot^{\circ}\text{C}$.

The universal gas constant is $R = 8.36 \text{ J/mol}\cdot^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Converting $R$ into calories, we use $1 \text{ cal} = 4.18 \text{ J}$:

$R = \dfrac{8.36}{4.18} \text{ cal/mol}\cdot^{\circ}\text{C} = 2 \text{ cal/mol}\cdot^{\circ}\text{C}$

Using Mayer's relation, the molar specific heat at constant volume is:

$c_v = c_p - R = 8 - 2 = 6 \text{ cal/mol}\cdot^{\circ}\text{C}$

The change in internal energy of the gas is given by:

$\Delta U = n c_v \Delta T$

$\Delta U = 5 \times 6 \times 10 = 300 \text{ cal}$

Answer: $300$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Heat is supplied to a diatomic gas at constant pressure. Then the ratio of $\Delta Q : \Delta U : \Delta W$ is _______.
questions.solution:
For a diatomic gas, the number of degrees of freedom is $f = 5$.

The molar heat capacity at constant volume is $C_v = \dfrac{f}{2}R = \dfrac{5}{2}R$.

The molar heat capacity at constant pressure is $C_p = C_v + R = \dfrac{7}{2}R$.

At constant pressure, the heat supplied is $\Delta Q = nC_p\Delta T = n\left(\dfrac{7}{2}R\right)\Delta T$.

The change in internal energy is $\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T = n\left(\dfrac{5}{2}R\right)\Delta T$.

The work done by the gas is $\Delta W = nR\Delta T = n\left(\dfrac{2}{2}R\right)\Delta T$.

The ratio $\Delta Q : \Delta U : \Delta W$ is $\dfrac{7}{2} : \dfrac{5}{2} : \dfrac{2}{2} = 7 : 5 : 2$.

Answer: $7 : 5 : 2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel contains $0.15$ m$^3$ of a gas at pressure $8$ bar and temperature $140°$C with $c_p = 3R$ and $c_v = 2R$. It is expanded adiabatically till pressure falls to $1$ bar. The work done during this process is _______ kJ. ($R$ is gas constant)
questions.solution:
Given $P_1 = 8$ bar $= 8 \times 10^5$ Pa, $V_1 = 0.15$ m$^3$, and $P_2 = 1$ bar $= 10^5$ Pa.

The adiabatic index $\gamma$ is given by:

$\gamma = \dfrac{c_p}{c_v} = \dfrac{3R}{2R} = 1.5$

For an adiabatic process, $P_1 V_1^\gamma = P_2 V_2^\gamma$.

$V_2 = V_1 \left( \dfrac{P_1}{P_2} \right)^{\dfrac{1}{\gamma}}$

$V_2 = 0.15 \times \left( \dfrac{8}{1} \right)^{\dfrac{1}{1.5}} = 0.15 \times 8^{\dfrac{2}{3}} = 0.15 \times 4 = 0.6$ m$^3$

The work done during the adiabatic expansion is:

$W = \dfrac{P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2}{\gamma - 1}$

$W = \dfrac{8 \times 10^5 \times 0.15 - 1 \times 10^5 \times 0.6}{1.5 - 1}$

$W = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^5 - 0.6 \times 10^5}{0.5}$

$W = \dfrac{0.6 \times 10^5}{0.5} = 1.2 \times 10^5$ J

$W = 120$ kJ

Answer: $120$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thermodynamic system is taken through the cyclic process $A B C$ as shown in the figure. The total work done by the system during the cycle $A B C$ is $\_\_\_\_$ J.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.solution:
From the P-V diagram: A(2,100), B(5,300), C(5,100) in Pa and m³ units.
Process A→B is linear. Equation: $P = 100 + \frac{200}{3}(V-2)$
$W_{AB} = \int_2^5 \frac{200V - 100}{3} dV = \frac{1}{3}[100V^2 - 100V]_2^5 = \frac{1800}{3} = 600$ J
Process B→C is isobaric: $W_{BC} = 300(5-5) = 0$ J
Process C→A is isobaric: $W_{CA} = 100(2-5) = -300$ J
Total work done by system: $W = 600 + 0 - 300 = 300$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the following $p-V$ diagram the equation of state along the curved path is given by $(V-2)^{2}=4 a p$ where $a$ is a constant. The total work done in the closed path is
questions.solution:
From the equation of state $(V-2)^2 = 4ap$, we get $p = \frac{(V-2)^2}{4a}$.
At V = 1: $p = \frac{1}{4a}$ and at V = 3: $p = \frac{1}{4a}$.
The curved path A→B→C follows the given equation, while C→A is a straight line at constant pressure.
Work along the curved path:
$W_{ABC} = \int_1^3 \frac{(V-2)^2}{4a} dV = \frac{1}{4a}\left[\frac{(V-2)^3}{3}\right]_1^3 = \frac{1}{4a} \cdot \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{6a}$.
Work along C→A at constant pressure:
$W_{CA} = \frac{1}{4a}(1-3) = -\frac{1}{2a}$.
Total work: $W_{total} = \frac{1}{6a} - \frac{1}{2a} = -\frac{1}{3a}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: 10 mole of an ideal gas is undergoing the process shown in the figure. The heat involved in the process from $P_{1}$ to $P_{2}$ is $\alpha$ Joule ($P_{1}=21.7 \mathrm{~Pa}$ and $\left.P_{2}=30 \mathrm{~Pa}, \mathrm{C}_{v}=21 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{K}. \mathrm{mol}, R=8.3 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{mol}. \mathrm{K}\right)$. The value of $\alpha$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
From the given $P-V$ diagram, the process from $P_1$ to $P_2$ is an isochoric process because the volume remains constant at $V = 1\text{ m}^3$.
For an isochoric process, the work done $W = 0$.
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the heat involved is $Q = \Delta U + W = \Delta U$.
The change in internal energy is given by $\Delta U = n C_v \Delta T$.
Using the ideal gas equation $PV = nRT$, we have $n\Delta T = \frac{V\Delta P}{R}$.
Substituting this into the expression for $Q$:
$Q = C_v \left( \frac{V(P_2 - P_1)}{R} \right)$
Given values: $n = 10$ moles, $V = 1\text{ m}^3$, $P_1 = 21.7\text{ Pa}$, $P_2 = 30\text{ Pa}$, $C_v = 21\text{ J/mol}\cdot\text{K}$, and $R = 8.3\text{ J/mol}\cdot\text{K}$.
$Q = 21 \times \frac{1 \times (30 - 21.7)}{8.3}$
$Q = 21 \times \frac{8.3}{8.3} = 21\text{ J}$.
Thus, the value of $\alpha$ is 21.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When 300 J of heat given to an ideal gas with $C_{p}=\frac{7}{2} R$ its temperature raises from $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ keeping its volume constant. If n is the number of moles of the gas, then what is the value of $100n$? $(\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{mol}. \mathrm{K})$
questions.solution:
Given: $C_P = \frac{7}{2}R$, so $C_V = C_P - R = \frac{5}{2}R$
$\Delta Q = nC_V \Delta T$ (constant volume)
$300 = n \times \frac{5}{2} \times 8.314 \times 30$
$n = 0.48$ mol
$100n = 48$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Density of water at $4{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ are $1000 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ and $998 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ respectively. The increase in internal energy of 4 kg of water when it is heated from $4{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is $\_\_\_\_$ J.
(specific heat capacity of water $=4.2 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{kg}$. and 1 atmospheric pressure $=10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$)
questions.solution:
Heat absorbed by water: $Q = mc\Delta T = 4 \times 4200 \times 16 = 268800$ J.
Volume change: $V_1 = 4/1000 = 0.004$ m³ at 4°C, $V_2 = 4/998 ≈ 0.00401$ m³ at 20°C.
Work done by water at constant pressure: $W = P_{atm}\Delta V = 10^5 \times 0.00001 = 0.8$ J.
By first law of thermodynamics: $\Delta U = Q - W = 268800 - 0.8 = 268799.2$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
One mole of an ideal diatomic gas expands from volume $V$ to 2 V isothermally at a temperature $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and does $W$ joule of work. If the gas undergoes same magnitude of expansion adiabatically from $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ doing the same amount of work $W$, then its final temperature will be (close to) $\_\_\_\_{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
$\left(\log _{\mathrm{e}} 2=0.693\right)$
questions.solution:
For isothermal expansion of 1 mole diatomic gas from V to 2V at 300 K:
$W = RT\ln 2 = R(300)\ln 2$
For adiabatic expansion with same volume change and same work output:
$W = nC_V\Delta T = C_V(T_i - T_f)$
For diatomic gas, $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$. Setting work equal:
$R(300)\ln 2 = \frac{5}{2}R(300 - T_f)$
Simplifying:
$300\ln 2 = 2.5(300 - T_f)$, so $300(0.693) = 2.5(300 - T_f)$
$207.9 = 750 - 2.5T_f$, giving $T_f = 216.84$ K $\approx$ -56°C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The internal energy of a monoatomic gas is 3 nRT. One mole of helium is kept in a cylinder having internal cross section area of $17 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ and fitted with a light movable frictionless piston. The gas is heated slowly by suppling 126 J heat. If the temperature rises by $4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, then the piston will move $\_\_\_\_$ cm.
(atmospheric pressure $=10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$)
questions.solution:
The question states the internal energy of the gas is $U = 3nRT$.
The change in internal energy is $\Delta U = 3nR\Delta T$.
Given: $n = 1$ mole, $\Delta T = 4^{\circ}C = 4$ K, and $R \approx 8.314$ J/mol·K.
$\Delta U = 3 \times 1 \times 8.314 \times 4 = 99.768$ J.
According to the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta Q = \Delta U + W$.
Given heat supplied $\Delta Q = 126$ J.
Work done by the gas $W = \Delta Q - \Delta U = 126 - 99.768 = 26.232$ J.
Since the piston is light and movable, the process occurs at constant atmospheric pressure $P = 10^5$ Pa.
Work done $W = P \Delta V = P(A \times d)$, where $A$ is the cross-section area and $d$ is the displacement of the piston.
$A = 17 \text{ cm}^2 = 17 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$.
$26.232 = 10^5 \times (17 \times 10^{-4}) \times d$.
$26.232 = 170 \times d$.
$d = \frac{26.232}{170} \approx 0.1543$ m.
Converting to cm: $d \approx 15.43$ cm.
Rounding to the nearest option, we get $15.5$ cm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An insulated cylinder of volume $60 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ is filled with a gas at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and 2 atmospheric pressure. Then the gas is compressed making the final volume as $20 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ while allowing the temperature to rise to $77^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The final pressure is $\_\_\_\_$ atmospheric pressure.
questions.solution:
$PV = nRT$
$\dfrac{P_1 V_1}{RT_1} = \dfrac{P_2 V_2}{RT_2}$
$\dfrac{2 \times 10^5 \times 60}{300} = \dfrac{P_2 \times 20}{350}$
$P_2 = \dfrac{2 \times 10^5 \times 7 \times 3}{6}$
$P_2 = 7 \times 10^5 = 7 \text{ atm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A diatomic gas $(\gamma=1.4)$ does 100 J of work when it is expanded isobarically. Then the heat given to the gas $\_\_\_\_$ J.
questions.solution:
For an isobaric process, the first law gives: $Q = \Delta U + W$.
For a diatomic gas with $\gamma = 1.4$, we have $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$ and $C_P = \frac{7}{2}R$.
Since $W = nR\Delta T = 100$ J for isobaric expansion, the change in internal energy is: $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T = \frac{5}{2}nR\Delta T = \frac{5}{2} \times 100 = 250$ J.
Therefore, $Q = 250 + 100 = 350$ J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: 10 mole of oxygen is heated at constant volume from $30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The change in the internal energy of the gas is $\_\_\_\_$ cal. (The molecular specific heat of oxygen at constant pressure, $C_{P}=7 \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{mol}.{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{R}=2 \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{mol}.{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.)
questions.solution:
Given: $n = 10$ mol,
$\Delta T = 40 - 30 = 10°C$,
$C_P = 7$ cal/mol·°C,
$R = 2$ cal/mol·°C

So internal energy increases

questions.q:
Heat is given to an ideal gas in an isothermal process.

A. Internal energy of the gas will decrease.

B. Internal energy of the gas will increase.

C. Internal energy of the gas will not change.

D. The gas will do positive work.

E. The gas will do negative work.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
From the first law of thermodynamics, heat supplied to the system Q, change in internal energy of the system ∆U and work done by the system W are related as:

Q=∆U+W

Since the process is isothermal, the temperature of the system is constant and therefore ∆U=0 (i.e., internal energy is constant). 

⇒Q=W

As heat is supplied to the system, Q is positive and therefore W is positive i.e., gas will do positive work.

Hence, correct options are C and D.

Reason R : First law of thermodynamics is based on law of conservation of energy.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the option given below :
options: A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
questions.solution:
The first law of thermodynamics is stated as dQ=dU-dW. Since dQ is heat supplied to the system and positive thus, dW is work done on the system, i.e., negative work.

We know that the first law of thermodynamics deals with work done, and heat energy supplied or removed from a system. Therefore, it is based on the conservation of energy. The  law states that energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another.

Statement 1: An inventor claims to have constructed an engine that has an efficiency of $30 \%$ when operated between the boiling and freezing points of water. This is not possible.
Statement 2: The efficiency of a real engine is always less than the efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between the same two temperatures.
options: Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is not the correct explanation of Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is the correct explanation of Statement 1.
questions.solution:
According to Carnot's theorem - no heat engine working between two given temperatures of source and sink can be more efficient than a perfectly reversible engine i.e. Carnot engine working between the same two temperatures.
Efficiency of Carnot's engine, $n=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}$ where, $T_1=$ temperature of source $T_2=$ temperature of sink

questions.q: A diatomic ideal gas is used in a Car engine as the working substance. If during the adiabatic expansion part of the cycle, volume of the gas increases from $\mathrm{V}$ to $32 \mathrm{~V}$ the efficiency of the engine is
questions.solution:
The efficiency of cycle is

\eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}

for adiabatic process

\text { TV }^{r^{-1}}=\text { constant }

For diatomic gas $\gamma=\frac{7}{5}$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{T}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1^{\gamma-1}=\mathrm{T}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2^{\gamma-1} \\
& \mathrm{~T}_1=\mathrm{T}_2\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_2}{\mathrm{~V}_1}\right)^{\gamma-1} \\
& \mathrm{~T}_1=\mathrm{T}_2(32)^{\frac{7}{5}-1} \\
&=\mathrm{T}_2\left(2^5\right)^{2 / 5} \\
&=\mathrm{T}_2 \times 4 \\
& \mathrm{~T}_1=4 \mathrm{~T}_2 . \\
& \eta=\left(1-\frac{1}{4}\right)=\frac{3}{4}=0.75
\end{aligned}
